points.title: Special honorific & humble verbs
points.meaning: いらっしゃる, 召し上がる, おっしゃる / 参る, いただく, 申す
structure: いる・行く・来る → いらっしゃる (honorific) / おる, 参る (humble)
食べる・飲む → 召し上がる / いただく
言う → おっしゃる / 申す
見る → ご覧になる / 拝見する
する → なさる / いたす
points.explanation:
Many everyday verbs have their own honorific and humble forms instead of the お〜になる / お〜する patterns. Honorific, for others: 先生がいらっしゃいました, "The teacher has arrived." Humble, for yourself: 田中と申します, "My name is Tanaka."

Learn them as vocabulary — they come up constantly in shops, offices and on the phone.
nuances: いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる and くださる conjugate irregularly: いらっしゃいます (not いらっしゃります).
いただきます before a meal is the humble いただく.
common_mistakes: Using honorific forms for yourself: 私がいらっしゃいます ✗ → 私が参ります.
Using humble forms for others: 先生が参りました ✗ → いらっしゃいました.

points.title: 〜ところ
points.meaning: about to / in the middle of / just did
structure: Dictionary form + ところだ (about to)
〜ているところだ (in the middle of)
points.explanation: ところ pins down the exact stage of an action. Dictionary form + ところ: about to (今から出かけるところです, "I'm just about to head out"). ているところ: in the middle of it (今ご飯を食べているところです). た-form + ところ: just finished (今駅に着いたところです, "I've just got to the station").
nuances: ちょうど often comes with it: ちょうど終わったところです.
たところ is more immediate than たばかり (next lesson).
common_mistakes: Mixing up the forms: 着くところ (about to arrive) vs. 着いたところ (just arrived).
Using ところ for events long in the past.

points.title: 〜たばかり
points.explanation:
た-form + ばかり says something happened recently, from the speaker's point of view: 日本に来たばかりです, "I've only just come to Japan." The actual time can be minutes or months — it's about how recent it feels.

It behaves like a noun: 買ったばかりの傘, 食べたばかりなので.
nuances: たところ is more precise and immediate; たばかり is about the feeling of recency.
Noun + ばかり means "nothing but" — an N3 use.
common_mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 来るばかり means something else.
Using たばかり for things long ago that don't feel recent.

points.title: 〜間／〜間に
points.meaning: while, during (the whole time) / at some point during
structure: Verb (ている) / Noun + の + 間 (the whole time)
points.explanation: 間 (あいだ) covers the whole period while something continues: 夏休みの間、ずっと実家にいました, "I stayed at my parents' the whole summer break." 間に means at some point within that period: 留守の間に泥棒が入りました, "A burglar broke in while I was out."
nuances: The verb before 間 is usually ている or a state.
うちに (next lesson) is similar to 間に but adds "while you still can".
common_mistakes: Using 間 for a one-off event: 寝ている間、電話がありました ✗ → 寝ている間に.
Dropping の after a noun: 休み間 ✗ → 休みの間.

points.title: 〜うちに
structure: Verb (dictionary / ている / ない) + うちに
points.explanation:
うちに means doing something while a condition still holds, before it changes: 温かいうちに食べてください, "Please eat it while it's warm." 若いうちに色々な国へ行きたい, "I want to travel while I'm young."

With a ない-form it means "before…": 暗くならないうちに帰りましょう.
nuances: It can also describe something that happened unnoticed over time: 話しているうちに眠くなった.
Compare 間に, which lacks the "before it's too late" feeling.
common_mistakes: Using 前に where うちに fits: 温かい前に ✗ → 温かいうちに.
Dropping の: 学生うちに ✗ → 学生のうちに.

examples.furigana: {若|わか}いうちに{色々|いろいろ}な{国|くに}へ{行|い}きたいです。

points.title: 〜までに
points.explanation:
までに marks a deadline — something happens at some point before it: 金曜日までにレポートを出してください, "Please hand in the report by Friday."

Compare まで (until), for something that continues up to that point: 五時まで図書館で勉強します.
nuances: A verb can be the deadline: 夏が来るまでに痩せたい.
までには adds emphasis: 七時までには帰ります.
common_mistakes: Using まで for a deadline: 金曜日まで出してください ✗ → 金曜日までに.
Using までに with a continuing action: 五時までに働きます ✗ → 五時まで.

comparisons.note: まで: until (continuing). までに: by (a deadline).

examples.english: I'll study at the library until five.

points.title: 〜まま
points.meaning: as it is, leaving something unchanged
points.explanation:
まま means a state stays unchanged while something else happens: 靴をはいたまま部屋に入らないでください, "Please don't come in with your shoes on." テレビをつけたまま寝てしまいました, "I fell asleep with the TV on."

The unchanged state is often one that should have changed.
nuances: そのまま means "as it is": そのままでいいですよ.
The verb before まま is usually in the た-form.
common_mistakes: Using the dictionary form: つけるまま ✗ → つけたまま.
Dropping の after a noun: 昔まま ✗ → 昔のまま.

examples.japanese: 靴をはいたまま部屋に入らないでください。

examples.english: It's fine as it is.

points.title: 〜なくて (reason)
structure: Verb (ない-form): drop い → くて
points.explanation:
なくて links a negative reason to its result, usually a feeling or situation: 試験に合格できなくて、残念です, "I'm disappointed I couldn't pass the exam." 友だちが来なくて、心配しました, "My friend didn't show up, so I was worried."

The second part is usually an emotion or state, not a request or intention.
nuances: It's the negative partner of the て-form reason: 遅れて、すみません.
ないで means "without doing" — a different use (next lesson).
common_mistakes: Using なくて for "without": 朝ご飯を食べなくて学校へ行った ✗ → 食べないで.
Following it with a request: わからなくて、教えてください ✗ → わからないので、教えてください.

comparisons.note: なくて gives a reason; ないで means "without".

examples.furigana: {試験|しけん}に{合格|ごうかく}できなくて、{残念|ざんねん}です。
examples.english: I'm disappointed I couldn't pass the exam.

examples.english: My friend didn't show up, so I was worried.

examples.english: I didn't understand the language, so I had a hard time.

examples.english: I couldn't sleep at night — it was rough.

points.title: 〜ないで (without)
points.explanation:
ないで means doing the main action without doing something else: 朝ご飯を食べないで学校へ行きました, "I went to school without eating breakfast." It can also mean "instead of": バスに乗らないで、歩いて帰りました.

It's the same form as ないでください, minus the request.
nuances: ずに (next lesson) means the same but sounds more formal.
Compare なくて, which gives a reason.
common_mistakes: Using なくて for "without": 傘を持たなくて出かけた ✗ → 持たないで.
Using the ます form: 食べませんで ✗ → 食べないで.

examples.english: I went out without an umbrella.

examples.english: Instead of taking the bus, I walked home.

examples.japanese: 辞書を使わないで読めますか。
examples.furigana: {辞書|じしょ}を{使|つか}わないで{読|よ}めますか。
examples.english: Can you read it without a dictionary?

examples.english: Yesterday I studied without sleeping.

points.title: 〜ずに
structure: Verb (ない-form minus ない) + ずに
points.explanation:
ずに means the same as ないで — "without doing" — but sounds more formal or written: 何も言わずに帰りました, "He went home without saying anything." Take the ない-form, drop ない, and add ずに.

The one irregular is する → せずに.
nuances: ず on its own (without に) is a literary connector: 何も食べず、寝た.
しないで and せずに mean the same; せずに is more formal.
common_mistakes: しずに ✗ → せずに.
Keeping ない: 食べないずに ✗ → 食べずに.

examples.japanese: 何も言わずに帰りました。
examples.furigana: {何|なに}も{言|い}わずに{帰|かえ}りました。
examples.english: He went home without saying anything.

valid_alternatives.note: 言わないで means the same but is more conversational. This review wants ずに.

examples.english: I took the exam without studying.
